Table 4 Example of an experimental item used in Experiment 1, testing immediate recall. Manipulated variables were location congruency, information position, and question type. Underlined elements indicate target information. L = locative PP; t = temporal PP; v = verb (predicate); s = subject (agent); o = object (patient).

and were introduced by v ('in/at') or na ('at/on/in'). Each location was manipulated to be either congruent or incongruent (yet still plausible) in the given context. Congruency was determined based on the norming study (see Section 3). Temporal PPs included names of days, months, or parts of the day. All sentences were semantically unambiguous, and all constituents had clear grammatical roles.

Each sentence was followed by a comprehension question testing recall of either the agent (Kdo to udělal 'Who did it?') or the location (Kde se to stalo? 'Where did it happen?'). These general formulations were chosen to avoid reactivating specific lexical items from the sentence (see Chromý & Vojvodić, 2024). Agents and locations were selected for comparison because they represent core and optional pieces of information (an argument and an adjunct) that can occur in the same sentence position in Czech due to its relatively free word order (see Section 2). The two word-order variants of our stimuli differed only in the relative position of the agent and the location.

Alliteration or rhyme was avoided because such features may facilitate recall (see e.g., Potter & Lombardi, 1990; A. J. S. Sanford et al., 2006).

Experimental items were combined with 72 filler sentences differing in structure and length, each followed by a comprehension question targeting different types of information. Three practice trials were included. In total, each participant read 99 sentences.

4.1.3 Procedure

The experiment was conducted online using the PC IbexFarm platform (Zehr & Schwarz, 2022). Participants received general instructions and provided an informed consent. Then, they filled out the same demographic questionnaire as in the norming study. They then completed three practice trials. After the final practice trial, a message indicated the end of the practice phase, and the main experiment was initiated via button press.

Sentences were presented in random order. Each sentence first appeared as a continuous series of underscores and was revealed in full after a spacebar press. Participants read at their own pace. After a second spacebar press, the sentence disappeared and an open-ended question appeared. All questions referred only to information explicitly stated in the sentence. Responses were typed and submitted with the Enter key, which also advanced the experiment. The experiment took approximately 20-30 minutes. Reaction times were recorded as the time between the spacebar press that revealed the sentence and the press that hid it and displayed the question.

4.2 Data coding

Because the comprehension questions were open-ended, responses were coded manually following criteria adapted from Chromý and Vojvodić (2024). Multiple response variants were accepted as correct if they clearly contained the target information, including proper-name variants, plural forms, standard or colloquial alternatives, and minor spelling or diacritic errors when the intended meaning was unambiguous. Prepositional changes were accepted only if the meaning was preserved. Semantically related but nonidentical words were coded as incorrect (e.g., v divadle 'in the theatre' instead of na jevišti 'on the stage'; v práci 'at work' or v pracovně 'in the study room' instead of v kanceláři 'in the office'). Additional non-target information was ignored.

For example, for the location v kuchyni 'in the kitchen', responses such as v kuchyni, kuchyně, stalo se to v kuchyni ('in the kitchen, kitchen, it happened in the kitchen') were coded as correct, whereas v domě ('in the house') or v koupelně ('in the bathroom') were coded as incorrect.

4.3 Data processing and analysis

After coding was completed, the dataset was checked and trimmed. First, we excluded one participant whose overall accuracy was below 50%. Second, we removed all extremely long reaction times (> 100 s) and extremely short reaction times (< 1000 ms). Note that these reaction times reflect the time needed to read the entire sentence and press the button to continue. Importantly, all responses following extremely short sentence-reading RTs were also excluded. After this trimming step, we removed one participant with more than 15% missing RTs and another participant whose RTs were completely missing due to a recording error in PC IbexFarm.

Next, RTs were log-transformed, and we calculated the value corresponding to 2.5 standard deviations above the mean. This value was then back-transformed to milliseconds (25,831.06 ms) and used as an upper cut-off for additional RT trimming. In total, 2.52% of RTs and 0.24% of accuracy data were removed.

For the accuracy analysis, we fitted logistic mixed-effects models with response correctness as the dependent variable. Question type served as a fixed effect, and congruency and position were entered in interaction within question type. We initially specified a model with random intercepts for participants and items, by-item random slopes for question type and congruency, and by-participant random slopes for question type, congruency, and position. Following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017), random slopes were removed sequentially and nested models were compared using likelihood-ratio tests. Slopes whose removal did not significantly reduce model fit were excluded, while random intercepts for participants and items were retained throughout. The final model included question type as a random slope for both participants and items.

For the analysis of RTs, we fitted linear mixed-effects models with log-transformed RTs as the dependent variable. Word order (LTVSO vs. STVLO) and congruency (congruent vs. incongruent) were included as fixed effects. We initially specified a model with random intercepts for participants and items and random slopes for word order and congruency for both random factors. Following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017), random slopes were removed sequentially and nested models were compared using likelihood-ratio tests. Slopes whose removal did not significantly reduce model fit were excluded, while random intercepts for participants and items were retained throughout.

The final model included a random slope for congruency for items only.

4.4 Results

Response accuracy for individual conditions is shown in Table 6 and Figure 1.

Significant congruency effects were observed for both locations and agents. Locations congruent with the given context were recalled more accurately than incongruent ones (β = -0.598, SE = 0.157, z = -3.798, p < 0.001). Moreover, when a sentence contained a congruent location, the corresponding agent was also recalled more accurately (β = 0.559, SE = 0.191, z = -2.930, p < 0.01). Information position did not have a significant effect on accuracy. Figure 2 shows the model estimated RTs (in milliseconds) for the sentences in Experiment 1. The analysis revealed a strong congruency effect: sentences containing an incongruent location were read more slowly (β = 0.089, SE = 0.012, t = 5.679, p < 0.001).

A weaker effect of word order also emerged, indicating that sentences with sentence-initial locations (LTVSO) were read slightly more slowly (β = 0.033, SE = 0.011, t = 2.961, p = 0.003).

4.5 Discussion

Experiment 1 revealed a robust congruency effect for both locations and agents.

Congruent locations were recalled more accurately than incongruent ones, and their presence also improved recall of agents. Reading-time data showed the same pattern: sentences containing incongruent locations were read more slowly than those with congruent ones. Moreover, slower processing was observed for sentences with locations in initial position compared to medial position.

The presentation format of Experiment 1-displaying each sentence in full-allowed participants to read relatively naturally, including the possibility of re-reading. However, this format also meant that RTs provided only a coarse-grained measure of processing, as each RT reflected the interval between the button press that revealed the entire sentence and the press that advanced to the comprehension question. Consequently, while the faster RTs for sentences with congruent locations suggested reduced processing difficulty, these findings required corroboration using a more fine-grained measure.

To address this limitation, we conducted Experiment 2, which used word-by-word presentation. This method provided a more detailed picture of online processing and allowed us to examine whether the congruency effect observed in Experiment 1 persists under conditions that prevent regressions and yield more localized reading-time measures.

5 Experiment 2

As in Experiment 1, Experiment 2 examined immediate recall from written sentences using a self-paced reading task. The only difference was in the mode of sentence presentation: instead of being shown as a whole, sentences were presented word-by-word.

Although this format lowers ecological validity, it provides more fine-grained insight into online processing during sentence reading.

5.1 Method

5.1.1 Participants

The initial sample comprised 184 Charles University students, none of whom took part in Experiment 1. The same exclusion criteria as in Experiment 1 were applied, resulting in the exclusion of one participant (see Data analysis). The resulting sample thus consisted of 183 participants (133 female, 47 male, 3 not disclosed; mean age = 23 years).

5.1.2 Materials

All experimental, filler, and practice items were identical to those used in Experiment 1.

5.1.3 Procedure

The procedure of Experiment 2 was identical to that of Experiment 1 except for the method of stimulus presentation. Each sentence initially appeared as a series of underscores. Pressing the spacebar revealed the first word; each subsequent press displayed the next word while the previous one disappeared, continuing until the entire sentence had been presented. After the final word, pressing the spacebar again triggered an open-ended comprehension question.

5.2 Data coding

Data coding was identical to that used in Experiment 1.

5.3 Data processing and analysis

As in Experiment 1, the data were first checked and trimmed. No participant showed response accuracy below 50%, so no one was excluded based on this criterion. We again removed extremely long and extremely short RTs. Because RTs in this experiment corresponded to individual words rather than entire sentences, we used 100 ms as the lower cut-off and 10 s as the upper cut-off. One participant was excluded for having more than 10% missing values after this initial trimming step.

As in Experiment 1, we then log-transformed all RTs and established an upper cut-off point corresponding to 2.5 standard deviations above the mean of the log-transformed distribution. After back-transforming, this threshold corresponded to 1371.7 ms, and all RTs above this value were removed. In total, 2.36% of RTs were excluded from the analysis.

For the accuracy analysis, we used the same logistic mixed-effects modeling procedure as in Experiment 1. Specifically, we initially specified a model with random intercepts for participants and items, by-item random slopes for question type and congruency, and by-participant random slopes for question type, congruency, and position.

Random slopes were then removed sequentially using likelihood-ratio tests following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017). The final model retained question type as a random slope for both participants and items.

Reaction-time analyses again employed linear mixed-effects models (Bates et al., 2014). A potential issue for the reaction-time analysis arises from the fact that the two word orders place the regions of interest (e.g., locations, agents) in different sentence positions, which complicates direct comparability. To address this, we fit two separate models.

(i) Target-word model. This model focused on RTs for the target word (location or agent). Depending on word order, the target word appeared either in sentence-initial position (locations in the LTVSO orders and agents in the STVLO orders) or in sentence-medial position (locations in the STVLO order and agents in the LTVSO order).

(ii) Sentence wrap-up model. This model focused on RTs for the final word of the sentence, i.e., the wrap-up effects (cf. Just & Carpenter, 1980; Kuperman et al., 2010; Rayner et al., 2000). These measures are crucial, as we assume that congruency reflects semantic integration of the sentence as a whole, rather than just a local fit of the target word at its position.

In both analyses, the dependent variable was the log-transformed RT, and participant and item were included as random effects. For the target-word model, fixed effects included the main effect of target region (location vs. agent) and two fixed effects nested under it: word order (LTVSO vs. STVLO) and congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), entered in interaction. For the sentence-final model, fixed effects were congruency and word order, also entered in interaction.

For the target-word model, we initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, by-participant random slopes for target region, word order, and congruency, and by-item random slopes for target region and congruency. Following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017), random slopes were removed sequentially and nested models were compared using likelihood-ratio tests. Slopes whose removal did not significantly reduce model fit were excluded, while random intercepts for participants and items were retained throughout. The final model retained target region as a random slope for both participants and items.

For the sentence wrap-up model, we initially specified random intercepts for par-ticipants and items and random slopes for congruency and word order for both random factors. The same model-selection procedure was then applied. The final model retained congruency as a random slope for participants.

5.4 Results

Response accuracy for individual conditions is presented in Table 6 and Figure 1.

The analysis revealed a strong congruency effect for locations and a weaker positional effect for agents. As in Experiment 1, congruent locations were recalled more accurately than incongruent ones (β = -0.891, SE = 0.153, z = -5.836, p < 0.001). For agents, recall was higher when the agent appeared in medial position compared to initial position (β = 0.541, SE = 0.165, z = 3.283, p = 0.001). No positional effect was observed for locations (β = -0.038, SE = 0.151, z = -0.250, p = 0.802).

The target-word model revealed a robust difference in RTs between agents and locations; we observed faster reading for locations compared to agents (β = -0.144, SE = 0.032, t = -4.549, p < 0.001). Agents in initial position (i.e., in the STVLO word order) were processed slower than agents in medial position (i.e., in the LTVSO word order) (β = -0.184, SE = 0.043, t = -4.27, p < 0.001). Importantly, no congruency effect and no difference between word orders for locations was documented as significant. The model estimates are plotted in Figure 3.

The sentence wrap-up model yielded a robust main effect of congruency with longer RTs at the wrap-up region for the incongruent condition: (β = 0.064, SE = 0.009, t = 6.385, p < 0.001). No other effects were significant. The model estimates are plotted in Figure 4

5.5 Discussion

Experiment 2 replicated the key finding from the Experiment 1: we again documented a robust congruency effect, with congruent locations being recalled more accurately than incongruent ones.

Importantly, the word-by-word presentation mode allowed us to examine the online processing of the sentences in greater detail. We found an effect analogous to that in Experiment 1, where entire sentences were processed more slowly when they contained incongruent locations. In Experiment 2, this slowdown emerged at the sentence wrap-up region. Interestingly, we did not find any effect on the words directly referring to the locations-there was no evidence that congruent and incongruent locations differed in RTs at the moment they were encountered. This finding is not surprising, as the whole sentence context was necessary to fully integrate the location and evaluate its congruency.

Another potentially interesting observation is that agents were processed more slowly than locations. However, we did not find a corresponding difference in recall accuracy between these two information types. One possible explanation is that nouns referring to locations were consistently preceded by a locative preposition, which may have facilitated processing of the subsequent word (cf. Ryskin & Nieuwland, 2023).

Unlike in Experiment 1, we observed a positional effect for agents, with better recall when agents appeared in medial position. We return to this finding in the General Discussion, where we compare patterns across all four experiments.

In sum, the congruency effect appears reliably in immediate recall. In the next two experiments, we turned to the question of whether congruency also influences later recognition. That is, we investigated whether information congruency affects longer-term retention. To address this question, we introduced a delayed word recognition task.

6 Experiment 3

Experiment 3 comprised two parts. The first part replicated Experiment 1, with minor procedural adjustments (see below). The second part introduced a delayed word recognition task to explore the influence of congruency on long-term information reten-tion.

6.1 Method

6.1.1 Participants

The final sample consisted of 240 Charles University students (191 female, 48 male, 1 not disclosed, mean age = 23 years). None of the participants had taken part in the previous experiments. No participants met the exclusion criteria, which were identical to those in Experiments 1 and 2.

6.1.2 Materials

All experimental and practice items in the first part of Experiment 3 were identical to those used in Experiment 1. The filler items were modified so that they did not contain any words appearing in the later word recognition task, nor their synonyms or semantically related terms since numerous studies have shown that people tend to store conceptual rather then verbatim information in long-term memory. (Bransford et al., 1972; Lombardi & Potter, 1992; Potter & Lombardi, 1990; Sachs, 1967; A. J. Sanford, 2002; A. J. Sanford & Garrod, 2005; Zwaan, 2016).

For the second part of the experiment, i.e., the delayed word recognition task, we constructed a list of 96 nouns in their lemma forms. The list included 48 nouns used as locations in the experimental items (24 congruent and 24 incongruent), 24 nouns used as agents (male and female proper names), and 24 additional male and female proper names that did not appear in the experimental items. Each participant had thus been exposed to half of the words from the list during the reading phase of the experiment, depending on the condition they received.

For each experimental item, the congruent and incongruent locations formed a pair associated with the same event description (e.g., forest vs. elevator in the item took a picture of a deer in the forest/elevator). Because participants encountered only one version of each item, some locations from these pairs served as new words in the recognition task.

6.1.3 Procedure

The first part of the experiment tested immediate recall, and its procedure closely followed that of Experiment 1 -it was a reading task with entire sentences presented at once, each immediately followed by a comprehension question. The only difference lied in the modified item order. The reading task always concluded with 12 filler items presented in random order, each followed by a comprehension question. This was intended to create a longer delay between the presentation of the experimental items and the subsequent recognition task. The delay represented a compromise between introducing a temporal separation from the immediate recall task and maintaining a feasible singlesession experimental procedure.

Unlike in Experiment 1, the demographic questionnaire was administered only after the reading phase had been completed, again to extend the delay before the word recognition task. The informed consent was obtained at the beginning of the experiment.

In the delayed word recognition task, participants were presented with a sequence of 96 nouns and indicated by clicking "yes" or "no" whether they had encountered each word in the first part of the experiment. The order of items was randomized individually for each participant. Importantly, half of the items were always new for each participant.

6.2 Data processing and analysis

Data processing for the reading data followed the identical procedure as in Experiment 1 (see Section 4.3). This time, no participant was excluded due to a large number of missing RTs after trimming or due to generally low response accuracy. The trimming procedure led to the exclusion of 2.53% of RT data and 0.18% of accuracy data. The upper cut-off was set to 22,360.69 ms.

Random-effects structures were selected following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017). Initial models included the maximal converging random-effects structure justified by the design, and simplified models were evaluated using likelihoodratio tests. Random slopes whose removal did not significantly reduce model fit were excluded, while random intercepts were retained throughout.

For the immediate recall accuracy analysis, we used the same fixed-effects struc-ture as in Experiment 1. We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, together with by-item and by-participant random slopes for question type and an additional by-participant random slope for congruency. The final model retained question type as a random slope for both participants and items.

For the RT analysis, we fitted linear mixed-effects models with log-transformed RTs as the dependent variable. Word order and congruency were included as fixed effects.

We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, by-participant random slopes for congruency, and by-item random slopes for congruency and word order. The final model retained congruency as a random slope for items only.

The analysis of recognition accuracy focused on several variables examining the effects of information type (agent, congruent location, incongruent location) and whether the noun had been presented to the participant during the experiment (old vs. new).

Agents were not further subdivided according to sentence congruency because congruency was manipulated at the level of the locations rather than the agents themselves.

Consequently, the primary recognition analyses classified agents as a single informationtype category. In the logistic mixed-effects model, recognition accuracy served as the dependent variable, while noun usage and information type were included as interacting fixed effects. Noun usage was treatment-coded with old items (i.e., words previously encountered by the participant) as the baseline, because our primary interest lay in differences in recognition among items that participants actually saw (i.e., in their retention).

For information type, we applied Helmert contrast coding (see Schad et al., 2020): the first contrast compared congruent versus incongruent locations, and the second contrast compared locations versus agents.

We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, together with random slopes for noun usage for both participants and items and a random slope for information type for items. Because removing the random slope for information type significantly reduced model fit, the initial random-effects structure was retained.

The final analysis examined the relationship between recall and recognition accuracies. For obvious reasons, we focused only on the subset of items that had been used in the reading task. In the logistic mixed-effects model, recognition accuracy served as the dependent variable. As fixed effects, information type (agent, congruent location, incongruent location) and recall accuracy (recalled vs. not recalled) were included in interaction. Information type was again Helmert contrast coded, and recall accuracy was sum contrast coded (recalled coded as -0.5 and not recalled as 0.5). We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items together with random slopes for recall accuracy for both participants and items. Alternative random-effects structures were evaluated, and the final model retained information type as a random slope for both participants and items.

6.3 Results

Table 6 and Figure 1 present recall accuracy for individual conditions. As in the previous experiments, a strong effect of congruency was observed for locations, with congruent locations recalled more accurately than incongruent ones (β = -0.531, SE = 0.139, z = -3.824, p < 0.001). A position effect was found for locations, with initial position leading to more accurate recall than medial position (β = -0.377, SE = 0.139, z = -2.719, p < 0.01).

Figure 5 presents the model estimated RTs (in milliseconds) for the sentences in Experiment 3. As in Experiment 1, the analysis revealed a strong congruency effect, with longer RTs for sentences containing incongruent locations (β = 0.109, SE = 0.015, t = 7.026, p < 0.001). The model also yielded a position effect, indicating that locations in initial position slightly slowed reading (β = 0.026, SE = 0.01, t = 2.688, p < 0.01).

Importantly, we failed to document any congruency effect for old locations.

The final analysis examined the extent to which the effects documented for delayed recognition can be explained by immediate recall. The logistic mixed-effects model yielded three significant effects on recognition accuracy: (i) a robust main effect of recall success-accuracy in the recognition task was higher for words that were previously recalled than for not recalled words (β = -2.044, SE = 0.122, z = -16.779, p < 0.001); (ii) a significant difference between locations and agents-agents were recognized less accurately (β = -0.234, SE = 0.053, z = -4.414, p < 0.001); and (iii) a weak interaction between location congruency and recall success-incongruent locations were recognized less accurately when previously not recalled (β = -0.362, SE = 0.158, z = -2.293, p = 0.022).

6.4 Discussion

Experiment 3 replicated most findings of previous experiments. We observed a strong congruency effect on immediate recall of locations, with congruent locations being recalled more accurately. Contrary to previous experiments, we documented a positional effect for locations (locations presented in the medial position were recalled less accurately than those at the beginning of a sentence), and we failed to replicate previously observed effects for agents. As in Experiment 1, we found effects of congruency and word order on RTs. Sentences containing congruent locations were read faster than those containing incongruent locations, and STVLO sentences were read faster than LTVSO sentences.

The delayed word recognition task yielded a robust effect of prior exposure: par-ticipants found it easier to correctly reject a word that had not appeared in the reading task (i.e. new) than to correctly accept a word that had appeared (i.e. old). Crucially, we did not observe any congruency effect for old locations. However, an interesting effect emerged for newly presented words-when these represented congruent locations, false alarms were more frequent than for incongruent locations or agents. This pattern may relate to findings by Haeuser and Grüter (2025) and Haeuser and Kray (2022 , 2023 , 2024 , 2026), who interpret similar effects as "false memories" stemming from highly predictable contexts. Interestingly, agents showed lower recognition accuracy than locations for old nouns, but higher recognition accuracy than locations for new nouns.

In addition, if a piece of information (i.e., location or agent) was successfully recalled immediately after reading a sentence, it was also accurately recognized later in the word list, suggesting the importance of initial encoding. Overall, locations were recalled more accurately than agents in both task types. Locations that were not recalled after reading yielded chance-level recognition, whereas agents were recognized even below chance. We return to this finding in the General Discussion. The delayed word recognition part remained unchanged.

7.1 Method

7.1.1 Participants

The final sample consisted of 181 Charles University students (130 female, 50 male, 1 not disclosed, mean age = 22.89 years), none of whom had participated in the previous experiments. No participants met the exclusion criteria, which were the same as in previous experiments.

7.1.2 Materials

All experimental, filler and practice items were identical to those in Experiment 3, as well as the word list for the delayed word recognition task.

7.1.3 Procedure

The procedure of the first part of Experiment 4 was identical to that of Experiment 2, i.e. a self-paced reading task with word-by-word presentation, followed by a comprehension question after each sentence. The order of items was modified in the same manner as in Experiment 3, with 12 filler sentences concluding the reading task, to create a time delay before the second part (i.e. the delayed word recognition task). The delayed recognition task was identical to that of Experiment 3 and included 96 location and agent nouns for which participants were asked to indicate whether they had encountered each word in the first part of the experiment by clicking "yes" or "no".

7.2 Data processing and analysis

Reading data were processed following the same procedure as in Experiment 2 (see Section 5.3). One participant was excluded due to low response accuracy, and no participants were excluded for excessive missing RTs after trimming. The trimming procedure resulted in the exclusion of 2.56% of RT data. The upper cut-off was set to 1,372.64 ms.

Unless stated otherwise, random-effects structures were selected following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017). Initial models included the maximal randomeffects structure justified by the design, and simplified models were evaluated using likelihood-ratio tests. Random slopes whose removal did not significantly reduce model fit were excluded, while random intercepts were retained throughout.

For the comprehension-accuracy analysis, we used the same fixed-effects structure as in Experiment 1. Random intercepts for participants and items and random slopes for question type for both random factors were specified. Because removing the item-specific random slope for question type significantly reduced model fit, the original random-effects structure was retained.

The analysis of RTs followed the approach used in Experiment 2. The target-word model examined RTs in the target regions. Fixed effects included target region (location vs. agent), word order (LTVSO vs. STVLO), and congruency (congruent vs.

incongruent). We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, byparticipant random slopes for target region, word order, and congruency, and by-item random slopes for target region and congruency. Because removing the random slope for word order for participants significantly reduced model fit, the original random-effects structure was retained.

The sentence wrap-up model analyzed RTs on the final word of the sentence. Fixed effects included congruency and word order in interaction. We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items together with a by-participant random slope for congruency. Because removing the random slope for congruency did not significantly reduce model fit, the final model contained only random intercepts for participants and items.

The analysis of recognition accuracy was identical to that used in Experiment 3.

Recognition accuracy served as the dependent variable, with noun usage (old vs. new) and information type included as interacting fixed effects. We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, together with random slopes for noun usage and information type for both random factors. Because removing the random slope for information type for participants did not significantly reduce model fit, this slope was excluded from the final model. The final model retained random slopes for noun usage for both participants and items and a random slope for information type for items.

As in Experiment 3, we also examined the relationship between recall and recognition accuracies. Recognition accuracy served as the dependent variable, with information type and recall accuracy included in interaction as fixed effects. We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items together with random slopes for information type for both random factors. Alternative random-effects structures were evaluated, and replacing the participant-specific random slope for information type with a random slope for recall accuracy significantly improved model fit. The final model therefore included a random slope for information type for items and a random slope for recall accuracy for participants.

7.3 Results

Table 6 and Figure 1 present response accuracy for individual conditions. A highly significant congruency effect was observed for locations, with congruent locations being recalled more accurately (β = -0.841, SE = 0.142, z = -5.916, p < 0.001), replicating the results of all previous experiments. The presence of a congruent location in the sentence also facilitated recall of agents (β = -0.406, SE = 0.142, z = -2.868, p = 0.004).

In addition, a positional effect was found for agents, with more accurate recall in medial position (β = 0.48, SE = 0.14, z = 3.421, p < 0.001).

The analysis of reaction times documented the following effects. As in Experiment 2, the target model showed a main effect of target region (β = -0.099, SE = 0.013, t = -7.913, p < 0.001), indicating that agents were read more slowly than locations, and agents were processed more slowly in the initial position (STVLO word order) than in the medial position (LTVSO word order; β = -0.038, SE = 0.010, t = -3.683, p < 0.001).

Contrary to Experiment 2, the model also yielded a weak effect of congruency for locations (β = 0.027, SE = 0.011, t = 2.426, p < 0.05), meaning that congruent locations were read faster. Moreover, we documented an interaction between congruency and word order for agents (β = 0.049, SE = 0.018, t = 2.750, p < 0.01), which appears to be driven by a speed-up in the congruent condition of the LTVSO word order. The model estimates are presented in Figure 7.

The sentence wrap-up model fully replicated the findings of Experiment 2, showing a robust main effect of congruency, with longer RTs in the incongruent condition at the wrap-up region (β = 0.050, SE = 0.009, t = 5.349, p < 0.001). No other significant effects were observed. The model estimates are visualized in Figure 8. were recognized more accurately when they referred to locations than to agents (β = -0.109, SE = 0.039, z = -2.774, p = 0.006), whereas new words were recognized more accurately when they referred to agents (β = 0.343, SE = 0.025, z = 14.057, p < 0.001).

The delayed recognition accuracy results are presented in

Lastly, new incongruent locations were recognized more accurately than new congruent locations (β = 0.313, SE = 0.05, z = 6.323, p < 0.001). As in Experiment 3, we failed to find an effect of congruency for locations that occurred in the reading task.

In the analysis of the role of recall success on subsequent recognition, we replicated two main effects found in Experiment 3: (i) recognition accuracy was higher for words that have been previously recalled immediately after reading the sentence than for words that have not been recalled (β = -2.17, SE = 0.138, z = -15.705, p < 0.001); and (ii) agents were recognized less accurately than locations (β = -0.167, SE = 0.044, z = -3.806, p < 0.001). Contrary to Experiment 3, we failed to document a significant interaction between location congruency and recall success. No other effects were significant.

To determine whether performance differed from chance, we again tested estimated marginal means (EMMs) against chance level (0.5) on the probability scale (two-sided, Holm-adjusted across six tests). By doing so, we replicated the results of Experiment 3. When items were not recalled, recognition of congruent locations (prob = 0.534, SE = 0.069, z = 0.488, p = 0.634) and incongruent locations (prob = 0.453, SE = 0.047, z = -1.001, p = 0.634) did not differ from chance, whereas the rate of misses for agents was even below chance (prob = 0.336, SE = 0.037, z = -4.44, p < 0.001). The recognition of items that were recalled directly after reading sentences, was always above the chance level: congruent locations (prob = 0.881, SE = 0.018, z = 21.118, p < 0.001), incongruent locations (prob = 0.889, SE = 0.014, z = 27.523, p < 0.001), and agents (prob = 0.844, SE = 0.014, z = 24.006, p < 0.001). These results are plotted in Figure

7.4 Discussion

Experiment 4 reinforces the central finding observed across the study: a robust congruency effect on immediate recall of locations, with congruent locations recalled more accurately. This pattern replicates Experiments 1-3 and supports the view that congruent information benefits rapid consolidation at the sentence level. We also documented two recall-related effects that were not consistently present in previous experiments -namely, a congruency effect for agents (also present in Experiment 1) and a positional effect for agents (also present in Experiment 2). Because the congruency effect for agents was not replicated across all experiments, we return to it in the pooled analysis and General Discussion, where its overall strength can be evaluated more reliably.

Regarding RTs, we replicated the main findings from the previous word-by-word experiment (Experiment 2). At the sentence wrap-up region, we again observed a speedup associated with location congruency. In the target regions, agents were read more slowly than locations, and agents were processed more slowly in the initial position than in the medial position. In addition, the present model yielded two effects not previously attested: (i) a weak congruency effect for locations, with congruent locations processed faster than incongruent ones (a borderline effect not observed in Experiment 2); and (ii) an interaction between congruency and word order for agents, driven by a speed-up for agents in the congruent condition under the LTVSO word order.

The delayed word recognition task reproduced the effects found in Experiment 3.

Words that had not appeared in the reading task (i.e., new) were recognized more accurately than those that had (i.e., old). For old words, agents were recognized less accurately than locations. For new words, the opposite tendency emerged: agents were more likely to be correctly rejected than locations, and incongruent locations were more likely to be correctly rejected than congruent locations-consistent with false-memory patterns observed in predictable contexts (Haeuser & Grüter, 2025; Haeuser & Kray, 2022 , 2023 , 2024).

Crucially, the analysis incorporating prior recall success yielded findings highly similar to Experiment 3: words recalled immediately after sentence presentation were later recognized with substantially higher accuracy than words that were not recalled.

Moreover, agents tended to be recognized less accurately than locations, irrespective of prior recall success. The only divergence from Experiment 3 in this analysis was the absence of a significant interaction between location congruency and recall success.

In sum, the main effects observed in previous experiments appear reliable and are replicated across studies. At the same time, several effects emerged selectively (e.g., agent congruency and agent positional effects), suggesting sensitivity to task parameters and presentation mode. To synthesize these outcomes, we next present the crucial analyses pooling data across all experiments, first examining recall patterns and then evaluating recognition accuracy in relation to recall.

8 Pooled analysis across experiments

For the pooled analysis of recall accuracy, we fitted a logistic mixed-effects model with recall accuracy as the dependent variable. The fixed-effects structure reflected the experimental design: question type served as the higher-level factor, and within each level of question type, we modeled the full interaction of location congruency, information position, and experiment type. Thus, the model tested whether the effects of congruency and position-and their interaction with presentation mode-varied across the two question types (agent-targeting and location-targeting).

Experiment type was a derived factor indicating the mode of sentence presentation during reading, with two levels: (i) word-by-word self-paced presentation (pooling Experiments 2 and 4) and (ii) whole-sentence presentation (pooling Experiments 1 and 3). It was treatment contrast coded with whole-sentence presentation being the baseline. Randomeffects structures were selected following the recommendations of Matuschek et al. (2017).

We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items, together with random slopes for question type and congruency for both random factors. Simplified models were evaluated using likelihood-ratio tests. Because removing the participant-specific random slope for congruency did not significantly reduce model fit, the final model retained random slopes for question type and congruency for items and a random slope for question type for participants.

The estimates from the model are presented in Figure For locations, the model yielded (i) a highly significant effect of congruency (β = -0.540, SE = 0.114, z = -4.754, p < 0.001), with congruent locations recalled more accurately than incongruent ones; (ii) a significant positional effect (β = -0.322, SE = 0.103, z = -3.133, p = 0.02), indicating that in whole-sentence presentation, locations in medial position were recalled less accurately than those in initial position; (iii) a weak effect of presentation mode (β = -0.255, SE = 0.101, z = -2.53, p = 0.011), suggesting that recall was worse after word-by-word presentation (Experiments 2 and 4) than after whole-sentence presentation (Experiments 1 and 3); (iv) a weak interaction between word-by-word presentation and congruency (β = -0.317, SE = 0.147, z = -2.161, p = 0.031), indicating that the congruency effect was more pronounced under word-by-word presentation; (v) an interaction between medial position and word-byword presentation (β = 0.383, SE = 0.146, z = 2.621, p = 0.009), suggesting that under word-by-word presentation, locations were recalled better in medial than in initial position; and (vi) a three-way interaction between congruency, medial position, and wordby-word presentation (β = 0.613, SE = 0.292, z = 2.096, p = 0.036), indicating that the congruency effect was larger in initial than in medial position under word-by-word presentation.

The pooled analysis of delayed recognition in relation to previous recall used a logistic mixed-effects model with recognition accuracy as a dependent variable, experiment (either Experiment 3 or Experiment 4), information type, and recall success as three fixed effects in interaction. Experiment was treatment contrast coded (with Experiment 3 as a baseline), information type was Helmert contrast coded as in Experiments 3 and 4 and recall success was sum contrast coded (recalled as -0.5 and not recalled as 0.5).

We initially specified random intercepts for participants and items together with random slopes for information type for both random factors. Alternative random-effects structures were evaluated using likelihood-ratio tests. Because including a participant-specific random slope for recall success significantly improved model fit, the final model included a random slope for information type for items and random slopes for information type and recall success for participants.

The model yielded two main effects: (i) agents were recognized to a lesser extent than locations (β = -0.162, SE = 0.049, z = -3.247, p = 0.001) and (ii) items that were recalled immediately after reading a sentence, had a significantly higher chance to be recognized in a delayed recognition task than items that were not recalled (β = -2.207,

9 General Discussion

The present study investigated how information congruency, information type, and sentence position influence memory during online sentence comprehension. Our central finding can be summarized as follows: Congruent information is consistently recalled better than incongruent information, but this advantage emerges only at the early stages of memory encoding. Crucially, this pattern was accompanied by a dissociation between immediate recall and delayed recognition. Across all four experiments, we observed a robust congruency advantage in immediate recall, whereas across both delayed-recognition experiments we found no reliable congruency advantage for previously encountered locations. This dissociation suggests that information congruency primarily influences the the developing situation model, resulting in both faster processing and higher recall accuracy. In contrast, the analysis including RT as a covariate examines variation within a given sentence type. Here, longer processing times likely reflect greater allocation of attention and more extensive encoding, which in turn improves memory performance.

Thus, RT appears to reflect both processing difficulty and encoding-related resource allocation. These influences operate in opposite directions across and within conditions, explaining why congruent sentences can be remembered better despite being processed more rapidly overall. Notably, RTs at the critical location and sentence-final wrap-up regions did not show a consistent relationship with recall across the word-by-word experiments, suggesting that this positive RT-memory relationship is not a general consequence of slower processing. Importantly, the congruency advantage in recall remained robust after controlling for RTs.

Although some studies report memory benefits for highly surprising or anomalous input, these effects tend to be secondary or population-specific (e.g., Haeuser & Kray, 2023; Höltje et al., 2019) and do not contradict the central finding that congruent information enjoys a substantial advantage in early memory.

9.2 No congruency advantage in delayed recognition

In contrast to the clear immediate recall pattern, delayed recognition (Experiments 3 and 4) showed no reliable congruency advantage for previously encountered locations.

Accuracy for congruent and incongruent locations was statistically indistinguishable in both experiments. Additional exploratory analyses examined whether delayed recognition depended on whether a word had originally appeared in a sentence with either congruent or incongruent location. This analysis was particularly relevant for agents, which were collapsed across location-congruency conditions in the primary recognition analyses. However, no reliable congruency effects were observed for either agents or locations in either experiment, further supporting the conclusion that congruency primarily affected immediate recall rather than later recognition.

The only significant effect related to location congruency in the delayed recognition task was observed in Experiment 3 and concerned the relationship with recall accuracy: when the information was not recalled immediately after reading a sentence, its later recognition was worse if it was incongruent rather than congruent. However, this effect was rather weak and was not present in Experiment 4. On the contrary, we failed to document any effect of location congruency if the information was recalled immediately after finishing reading. Our results suggest that incongruent information faces greater difficulty during the formation of a stable memory representation. However, once such a representation is successfully established, its later accessibility appears largely independent of the original congruency manipulation.

This pattern has broader implications for theories linking language comprehension and memory. Accounts of discourse comprehension often assume that readers construct a situation model that integrates incoming information with world knowledge and the evolving event representation (e.g., Ericsson & Kintsch, 1995; Zwaan, 2016). From this perspective, congruent information may benefit from easier integration into the developing model, increasing the likelihood that it will be successfully encoded and subsequently available for immediate recall. However, our results suggest that once information has been incorporated into that representation, its later recognition appears largely insensitive to its original degree of congruency. The critical role of congruency therefore appears to lie primarily in determining whether information becomes part of the encoded representation in the first place, rather than in determining the long-term accessibility of information that has already been encoded.

Importantly, this interpretation makes the absence of a congruency effect in delayed recognition theoretically informative rather than merely a null result. If congruency continued to influence memory representations after successful encoding, one might expect a delayed-recognition advantage for congruent locations. Across two experiments, however, we found no evidence for such an advantage. Notably, this absence of an effect was observed despite the robust and highly replicable congruency advantage in immediate recall. The data therefore suggest that congruency mainly influences the establishment of memory traces during comprehension, whereas later retrieval depends primarily on whether a sufficiently robust representation was formed.

However, congruency strongly influenced false alarms: new (unused) congruent locations-i.e., locations that were not presented to a participant but represented the congruent alternative within a given item pair-were more likely to be incorrectly accepted as old (used) than incongruent ones. This pattern implies that when the verbatim trace was no longer available, participants relied on contextual cues and world knowledge (cf. Roediger et al., 2001). They appear to have inferred plausible locations from the remembered event structure. This process also manifested in immediate recall, where some participants supplied a more congruent but unpresented location. For example, for the sentence Eliška v létě zorganizovala v továrně moc příjemnej narozeninovej piknik.

('Eliška organised a really nice birthday picnic in the factory in the summer.'), some participants reconstructed the location as v parku ('in the park') or v přírodě ('in the nature'), which is more congruent, instead of reporting the presented location v továrně ('in the factory'). The delayed recognition task amplified such reconstruction-based errors, yielding more false alarms for congruent new nouns, i.e., false memories (e.g., Haeuser & Grüter, 2025; Haeuser & Kray, 2022).

9.3 Impact of location congruency on immediate recall of agents

Unexpectedly, two experiments (Experiments 1 and 4) showed that agents were also recalled more accurately immediately after reading a sentence that contained a congruent (vs. incongruent) location. Because this effect occurred in both whole-sentence and word-by-word presentation, it cannot be attributed to re-reading (cf. Christianson et al., 2017; Speer & Clifton, 1998) which is not possible in the latter presentation mode.

Instead, it may reflect a more general increase in comprehension demands when the sentence contains an incongruent element (cf. Haeuser & Kray, 2023; Huettig, 2015), which reduces the availability of all other information in the sentence. The fact that this effect was not consistent across all experiments suggests that additional, uncontrolled factors contributed to this variability. The pooled analysis provides the most reliable assessment of its overall magnitude and suggests that any congruency-related benefit for agent recall is substantially weaker and less robust than the corresponding effect for locations.

9.4 Information type: agents versus locations

Contrary to our prediction, agents were not consistently recalled better than locations immediately after finishing reading. Only a marginal advantage emerged in the pooled analysis of whole-sentence presentation. Nonetheless, reading-time data revealed a reliable processing asymmetry: agents were read more slowly than locations. Previous work has often interpreted such asymmetries in terms of deeper processing of verbal arguments relative to adjuncts (Brown, 2008; Chromý & Vojvodić, 2024; Speer & Clifton, 1998). However, the comparison between agents and locations should be interpreted cautiously. Although agents and locations differed in their discourse status (argument vs.

adjunct), they also differed lexically, as agents were realized as proper names whereas locations were common nouns. This design choice was motivated by the need to avoid introducing additional congruency differences associated with the agents themselves, but it limits the extent to which observed differences can be attributed specifically to argument status.

One possible explanation for the observed pattern is that locations benefited from being introduced by highly predictive locative prepositions, whereas agents were represented by proper names whose identity was less constrained by the preceding context.

Differences between proper names and common nouns in lexical accessibility, or memorability may therefore have contributed to the observed recall and recognition patterns.

The delayed recognition results are also compatible with this possibility, as locations were recognized more accurately than agents, whereas new agents were rejected more reliably than new locations.

9.5 Information position

Position effects were weak and inconsistent across experiments, which is not surprising given that the position manipulation in the present study was secondary and primarily served to enable comparison of the tested information types. The design was therefore not well suited for a comprehensive test of position-based theories.

9.6 Limitations

One design trade-off in the present study concerned the number of experimental items. We deliberately maintained a relatively low proportion of experimental sentences and a high filler-to-experimental ratio. Previous work using the same immediate recall paradigm has shown robust task-adaptation effects, with recall accuracy increasing throughout the experiment as participants become familiar with the task demands (Chromý & Tomaschek, 2024). Increasing the number of experimental items would therefore likely have increased participants' awareness of the critical manipulations and encouraged task-specific memory strategies.

For this reason, each experiment contained 24 experimental items and 72 fillers.

Although this design reduced the number of observations per condition, it helped preserve the intended balance between experimental and filler items and minimized strategic adaptation. Moreover, each experiment included a comparatively large participant sample, and the critical congruency effect replicated across all four experiments and was confirmed in the pooled analysis. Nevertheless, some secondary effects (such as effects of information position) were less consistent across experiments and should therefore be interpreted with greater caution until replicated in future studies.

Another limitation concerns the relationship between congruency and plausibility.

The norming study measured perceived expectedness/congruency rather than plausibility, and plausibility was not assessed independently. Although care was taken to avoid impossible event descriptions, some variation in plausibility may have remained within both the congruent and incongruent conditions. Future studies could address this issue by collecting separate plausibility ratings and explicitly dissociating expectedness from plausibility.

10 Conclusions

Taken together, our results demonstrate that information congruency influences memory during the earliest stages of comprehension. Congruent locations benefited from facilitated encoding, yielding higher immediate recall accuracy, whereas incongruent locations led to increased processing effort without enhancing memory. In delayed recog-nition, the congruency advantage disappeared. These findings underscore that linguistic information is not uniformly encoded: congruency, argument status, and contextual constraints jointly shape how incoming material is processed, integrated, and remembered.

9.1 Congruency facilitates immediate memory

Across all experiments, we observed a robust congruency advantage in immediate recall: locations that fitted naturally with the described event were recalled more accurately than those that did not. This replicates and extends previous findings showing that congruent information is both processed more fluently (Luke & Christianson, 2016; Staresina et al., 2009; Van Kesteren et al., 2013; Volín & Šturm, 2023) and encoded more effectively into memory (Höltje et al., 2019; Staresina et al., 2009; Van Kesteren et al., 2013). These patterns are consistent with theories proposing that congruent input benefits from richer schema-based integration (Van Kesteren et al., 2013) or the construction of stronger semantic representations (Staresina et al., 2009).

Self-paced reading times provided complementary evidence. In both experiments which employed word-by-word presentation mode, we documented faster reading in sentencefinal regions (i.e., wrap-up effect, see Just & Carpenter, 1980; Kuperman et al., 2010; Rayner et al., 2000) for sentences containing congruent locations, indicating reduced information integration demands. The whole-sentence experiments showed the same pattern-sentences containing congruent locations were read faster than sentences containing incongruent locations. These results align with previous findings that predictable or contextually coherent words ease processing (Huettig, 2015; Luke & Christianson, 2016; Speer & Clifton, 1998).

Crucially, however, the congruency advantage in memory could not be explained solely by differences in processing time. Additional analyses relating RTs to recall performance revealed that longer sentence-level processing times were associated with better memory in the whole-sentence experiments (both ps < .01). At first glance, this pattern may appear inconsistent with the finding that congruent sentences were both processed faster and recalled more accurately. However, the two analyses address different sources of variation. Comparisons between congruent and incongruent sentences primarily capture differences in integration difficulty: congruent information is easier to integrate into
